UnitStatement: This scope-change brief describes how OpenPipeStress_PRD_v0.2.md differs from the earlier PRD.md, written for software-development agents changing OpenPipeStress's scope of work.
The new PRD does not remove the piping stress analytical engine; it preserves the ambition of a serious piping stress engine.
The product is no longer scoped as a standalone free and open-source piping stress analysis platform as in the original PRD.
The new PRD scopes the product as an analysis-grade piping design engine and stress-model authoring environment that uses a full internal solver for design iteration.
The product produces handoff-ready model data for downstream professional validation.
The original PRD positioned the product around global piping flexibility and stress analysis.
The new PRD positions the product around design knowledge, schema-backed physical modeling, GUI/agent-assisted iteration, state comparison, and prover-tool handoff.

Primary development instruction: keep building the serious piping stress engine but move the architecture from solver+GUI+reports to schema-backed design model + solver + GUI + model states + comparison + handoff workflow.
The original PRD described OpenPipeStress as a free and open-source piping stress analysis platform.
The original product vision was to become the leading transparent, auditable, code-neutral, open-source platform for piping flexibility and stress analysis.
The original core concept is open mechanics in the solver with user-owned code knowledge held in private data and rule packs.
The new PRD describes OpenPipeStress as an analysis-grade piping design engine and stress-model authoring environment.
The new PRD states the product is not intended to become an industry-standard professional stress-analysis platform or replace authenticated commercial software.
The product operates earlier in the design workflow, where routes, supports, constraints, equipment interfaces, and design assumptions are still evolving.
Future development should not treat the product as merely an open-source CAESAR II or AutoPIPE substitute; it should support a broader design-authoring workflow.

The intended design-authoring workflow proceeds: design knowledge to physical model to analytical model to internal solve to route/support iteration to saved model states to comparison to handoff package to external validation by a professional tool.
The solver remains core but is no longer the whole product.
The original PRD already included non-goals: it would not claim ASME certification, would not replace the responsible engineer, and would not provide automatic legal interpretation of piping codes.
The product boundary is not defined by solver capability; OpenPipeStress shall have a full analytical engine, and the boundary is defined by claim authority.
Governing distinction: OpenPipeStress computes and helps design, the external prover tool validates for reliance, and the responsible engineer accepts.
Do not weaken the solver because the tool is non-authoritative; the solver should still be correct, deterministic, benchmarked, and useful.
UI labels, reports, exports, comparison screens, agent output, and documentation must avoid language implying final approval, certification, code compliance for reliance, or professional acceptance.
The original PRD required project files, a model tree, a property editor, GUI modeling, and round-trippable data, but described the model mostly as a stress-analysis input file.
The new PRD makes the schema-backed physical model the central source of truth and distinguishes three model layers: physical model, analytical model, and handoff model.
The physical model is richer than the analytical model, including geometry, components, supports, constraints, equipment interfaces, provenance, unresolved assumptions, and design intent.
The analytical model is the idealized solver-ready representation; the handoff model is the target-specific export representation.
Future agents should implement model architecture as layered data, not as one flat solver input schema.

Required architecture shift: from project file to solver model to results/report, toward physical model to analytical transform to solver run to result state, plus handoff transform to downstream package.

The physical model should support design entities that may not directly appear in the solver, such as routing corridors, no-go volumes, supportable zones, design knowledge records, unresolved assumptions, and agent operation rationale.
The original PRD focused on materials, components, load cases, private rule packs, solver inputs, and reports, and did not define a broad design knowledge layer.

The new PRD adds a full Design Knowledge concept including line lists, P&ID-derived connectivity, equipment/nozzle locations, pipe specifications, routing corridors, no-go volumes, rack elevations, supportable structural zones, valve access, slope/drain/vent requirements, insulation/clearance envelopes, construction constraints, owner preferences, and stress-review triggers.

The new PRD adds a constraint engine for connectivity, endpoint matching, supportable span ranges, clearance envelopes, no-go volumes, slope requirements, drain/vent logic, valve access zones, supportable structure zones, and missing required data.
Add new domain modules beyond the stress solver: design_knowledge, constraints, routing_context, support_zones, equipment_interfaces, clearance_volumes, and provenance.
The GUI should allow users to enter, inspect, and validate design constraints, and future route/support generation should consume this layer rather than inventing geometry directly.

The original GUI requirements included a 3D centerline viewport, model tree, property inspector, material and component library editors, load-case manager, rule-pack manager, solver console, results browser, and report generator.

The new GUI scope adds operation history, a design knowledge panel, a constraint/warning panel, a model state and analysis run browser, a comparison browser, comparison overlays, routing corridors, no-go volumes, supportable zones, and model-state overlay comparisons.
The GUI should be designed as an interactive model authoring environment, not only as a stress-input editor.
The viewport must support analysis overlays: deformed shape, reactions, displacements, stresses, and terminal loads.
The viewport must support design overlays: route corridors, forbidden zones, support zones, clearance envelopes, changed entities, and comparison overlays.
The expanded GUI scope likely affects scene graph design, entity selection, property binding, undo/redo, operation history, and model-state visualization.
The original PRD did not meaningfully include agent-assisted design; it focused on human GUI workflow, rule packs, solver, validation, and reports.

The new PRD adds an agent-enhanced workflow where agents may propose route/support/model changes, but proposals must become structured model operations, pass schema and constraint validation, be shown as diffs, and require user acceptance unless configured otherwise.
Do not let agent features mutate the model through free-form text or hidden side effects.
Implement an operation pipeline: agent/user instruction to proposed model operation to schema validation to constraint validation to diff preview to user accept/reject to committed model state.
Future development should introduce a formal operation model early, even before advanced agents exist.
Example operation categories: add_route_segment, move_node, insert_bend, add_support, change_support_type, modify_pipe_section, add_no_go_volume, assign_material, and revise_load_case.
The original PRD required create/open/save/version projects and reproducible reports but did not define immutable model states or analysis runs as first-class entities.
Model State is defined as a named, immutable snapshot of a model at a point in time.
Analysis Run is defined as a solver execution attached to a specific model state.
Comparison is defined as a deterministic diff between two model states and/or two analysis runs.
Each analysis run must bind to exact model state, solver version, settings, units, load cases, and rule-pack/library references.
The persistence model needs to support immutable snapshots and run records, not just mutable project files.
A Project contains ModelState records, each with PhysicalModel, AnalyticalInputBasis, Assumptions, Warnings, and Hash.
A Project contains AnalysisRun records, each with model_state_id, solver_version, settings, load_cases, diagnostics, results, and results_hash.
Model state and analysis run infrastructure also affects report generation, reproducibility, comparison, undo/redo, export, and validation.

The original PRD included validation benchmarks, report reproducibility, and possible commercial software comparison as an open question, but no product feature for comparing model states or analysis result sets.

The new PRD adds a generic deterministic comparison tool that compares two model states and optionally two analysis runs using stable IDs, manual mappings, unit-normalized quantities, and tolerance profiles.
The comparison tool is explicitly not a comprehensive external-prover result ingestion platform in the MVP.

Add a compare subsystem responsible for state diffs covering added/removed/changed entities, geometry changes, topology changes, support changes, load changes, material changes, solver-setting changes, and warning/assumption changes.
The compare subsystem must produce result diffs covering displacement, rotation, force/moment, support reaction, equipment terminal load, stress/result, and diagnostics deltas.
Entity mapping must support at least stable ID match, manual user mapping, and unmatched/added/deleted classification.
Future external result comparison should be accommodated architecturally but not implemented as an MVP dependency.
In the original PRD, import/export was a secondary goal or Could requirement, and CAD/BIM/CAE exchange and commercial software comparisons were future or open-ended topics.
The new PRD defines an external prover tool as an accepted professional stress-analysis platform used outside OpenPipeStress to validate results for project reliance.

The new PRD defines a handoff package containing canonical model data, units manifest, entity IDs, library references, rule references, unresolved assumptions, warnings, hashes, and target mapping metadata.
The MVP explicitly does not include comprehensive external commercial tool result ingestion, forced prover status lifecycle, or automatic professional acceptance records.
Implement export/handoff infrastructure before building target-specific commercial-tool parsers.

Near-term handoff scope: canonical schema export, handoff manifest, model hash, units manifest, entity ID manifest, library/rule references, warnings, unresolved assumptions, target mapping metadata where known, and unsupported-target flags.
Deferred handoff scope: CAESAR II output parser, AutoPIPE output parser, automatic prover validation status, formal approval lifecycle, and commercial-tool result reconciliation.
Future agents should not overbuild external integration prematurely.
The original PRD had no prover-status lifecycle but did have report signoff, disclaimers, and professional limitations.

The new PRD explicitly says the MVP shall not force a formal prover-status vocabulary or lifecycle; instead users can use model names, state names, tags, notes, external reference fields, attachments/links, and comparison reports.
Do not build a rigid approval workflow in the MVP.
Implement flexible metadata instead: state.name, state.tags, state.notes, state.external_references, comparison.name, and report.notes.

Avoid hard-coded statuses such as PROVER_VALIDATED, APPROVED, CERTIFIED, CODE_COMPLIANT, and READY_FOR_CONSTRUCTION because they create professional-boundary risk and are contrary to the chosen scope.

The original PRD used a single functional requirements table FR-001 through FR-025 covering project files, units, modeling, solver, rule packs, GUI, reports, components, nonlinear supports, import/export, dynamic modules, and local FEA export.

The new PRD reorganizes requirements into domain groups: FR-MOD model and schema, FR-KNOW design knowledge and constraints, FR-GUI graphical interface, FR-SOL analytical engine, FR-RULE rule packs and private data, FR-CMP model state/analysis run/comparison, FR-HAND handoff and export, FR-AGENT agent-assisted design, and FR-REP reporting.
Future work breakdown should follow these subsystem boundaries; the new PRD is better suited for modular architecture and backlog creation.
The likely repository/module structure should expand beyond the original core, rules, gui, reports, and validation directories.
The expanded module structure should include schema, physical_model, analytical_model, model_transform, design_knowledge, constraints, operations, states, runs, comparison, handoff, and agents.
The new PRD retains core solver commitments: six-degree-of-freedom nodes, 3D frame/line-element analysis, straight pipe elements, rigid elements, and linear supports/restraints.
The new PRD retains load cases, weight/thermal/pressure-metadata/imposed-displacement loads, force/moment recovery, and fundamental stress recovery.
The new PRD retains bends, branches, valves, flanges, reducers, expansion joints, nonlinear restraints, and singularity and ill-conditioning diagnostics.
The solver is now explicitly embedded in a broader design workflow: the analytical model is derived from the physical model, and results attach to analysis runs tied to immutable model states.
Do not interpret v0.2 as reducing solver seriousness.
Implementation priority: solver correctness remains mandatory, and solver inputs/outputs must be state-bound, traceable, comparable, and exportable.
The analytical engine should be developed with stable serialization, result schemas, reproducibility, comparison, and handoff in mind from the beginning.
The original post-MVP scope included dynamic modules (modal, response spectrum, harmonic, time-history) and dynamic analysis was a Could requirement in the functional requirements table.

The new PRD does not emphasize dynamic analysis in the main roadmap; later modules may add dynamics, but release milestones focus on schema, solver, GUI, states/runs/comparison, rule packs/private libraries, piping components/nonlinear supports, design knowledge/handoff, and agent-assisted design.
Dynamic analysis should be deferred unless specifically reprioritized.

Near-term development should favor state/run infrastructure, comparison, physical-to-analytical transformation, handoff manifests, design constraints, and GUI model authoring over modal analysis, response spectrum, harmonic response, and time history.
The original release path was R0 Architecture Prototype, R1 Core Solver MVP, R2 GUI MVP, R3 Rule-Pack and Private Libraries, R4 Piping Components and Nonlinear Supports, and R5 Engineering Beta.

The new roadmap is R0 Schema and Solver Prototype, R1 Core Analytical Engine MVP, R2 GUI and Physical Model MVP, R3 States/Runs/Generic Comparison, R4 Rule Packs and Private Libraries, R5 Piping Components and Nonlinear Supports, R6 Design Knowledge and Handoff Beta, and R7 Agent-Assisted Design and Candidate Generation.
Two new major releases were inserted: R3 states/runs/comparison, R6 design knowledge/handoff, and R7 agents/candidate generation.

Rule packs move later relative to comparison; the project should not rush from solver/GUI into rule packs and components without first establishing model-state persistence and comparison infrastructure.

The new MVP adds canonical project schema, local-first storage, named immutable model states, analysis runs tied to states, basic model-state comparison, basic analysis-run comparison, export of a canonical schema-compliant model package, IP/data-boundary notices, and professional-boundary notices.

The MVP still includes 3D six-degree-of-freedom nodes, straight pipe/beam elements, rigid elements, anchors and linear restraints, weight loads, thermal loads, pressure metadata, and imposed displacements.

The MVP still includes a linear static solver, force/moment recovery, fundamental stress recovery, a basic GUI modeler, a private rule-pack schema with non-code examples, missing-data blockers, report generation, and a validation suite.

The new PRD explicitly excludes from MVP: comprehensive external commercial tool result ingestion, forced prover-status lifecycle, protected standards data, automatic professional acceptance records, and advanced nonlinear/dynamic modules unless otherwise prioritized.
The MVP is now more architecture-heavy, needing durable data modeling and reproducibility earlier; the main added implementation burden is model lifecycle infrastructure rather than numerical work.
The original PRD focused on calculation reports with model summaries, load cases, rule-pack checksums, warnings, results, and signoff blocks.

The new PRD expands reports to include model summary reports, analysis result reports, warning and assumption reports, user-rule check reports, model state comparison reports, analysis run comparison reports, and handoff package manifests.

The new PRD includes a stronger report notice identifying the software as decision-support software that does not certify, seal, approve, authenticate, or determine code compliance for professional reliance.
Reports should be generated from state/run/comparison/handoff records, not only from the current mutable project model.
Report generator inputs should include model_state_id, analysis_run_id, optional comparison_id, optional handoff_package_id, rule_pack checksum, library references, warnings, assumptions, and hashes.
The original PRD included solver benchmarks, stress recovery benchmarks, regression testing, and a validation manual.
The new PRD adds tests for schema round-trip, model state hashing, analysis run reproducibility, comparison output determinism, and report reproducibility.
The new PRD reframes external professional tool comparisons as optional validation evidence, not automatic professional acceptance.
CI/test planning must cover persistence and lifecycle behavior, not just solver math.

Add regression tests: same model state plus same solver version yields same result hash; same pair of states plus same mapping/tolerances yields same comparison output; schema serialize/deserialize yields no loss of typed data; report generation from the same state/run yields reproducible report metadata.
The original PRD had strong IP/data restrictions: no ASME text, tables, B31J content, B16/B36 tables, protected examples, or commercial software material without permission.

The new PRD aligns IP/data restrictions with the IP/Data Boundary Policy: the public repository may contain open solver algorithms, schemas, blank templates, invented example data, permissively licensed data, validation benchmarks, and private-library import mechanisms.

The public repository must not contain protected standards data, proprietary vendor catalogs without rights, commercial software examples without permission, private rule packs, owner standards, or protected code-specific acceptance criteria.
Continue implementing private-by-default rule packs, libraries, provenance metadata, and protected-content quarantine workflows.

Provenance and private-data handling now also apply to design knowledge, constraints, handoff packages, comparison reports, agent rationale, and external references, not only materials, components, and rule packs.
The original personas were piping stress engineer, owner-operator reviewer, engineering company administrator, open-source contributor, and educator/researcher.
The new personas include piping designer / layout engineer, piping stress engineer, owner-operator reviewer, engineering company administrator, open-source contributor, and agent-enhanced user.
The educator/researcher persona is no longer a primary persona, though educational/research examples remain a secondary goal.
UX should support design iteration, not just stress-calculation report preparation.

Prioritize workflows like create route, place supports, inspect constraints, run analysis, modify support, save new state, compare before/after, and export handoff over only build stress model, run code check, and issue calculation report.

The new PRD does not carry over original sections on detailed platform/technical architecture directory layout, performance requirements, accessibility and usability requirements, explicit source notes and external ASME reference pages, and detailed technology selection criteria.
Omission of those sections does not mean the requirements are invalid; v0.2 focused on product scope and workflow realignment.
Future agents should not assume performance, accessibility, or architecture concerns are abandoned; they should be reintroduced in a future technical architecture document or v0.3 PRD.

Recommended follow-up artifacts: TECHNICAL_ARCHITECTURE.md, DATA_MODEL_SPEC.md, COMPARISON_ENGINE_SPEC.md, HANDOFF_PACKAGE_SPEC.md, GUI_UX_REQUIREMENTS.md, PERFORMANCE_REQUIREMENTS.md, ACCESSIBILITY_REQUIREMENTS.md, and AGENT_OPERATION_SPEC.md.

Epic 1 Canonical Physical Model Schema: implement a schema representing physical entities, analytical entities, constraints, design knowledge, provenance, warnings, assumptions, external references, and stable IDs.

Epic 2 Physical-to-Analytical Transformation: implement deterministic transformation from physical model to solver model, including warnings when physical design data cannot be represented analytically.
Epic 3 Model States and Analysis Runs: implement immutable snapshots, result records, hashes, and reproducibility metadata.
Epic 4 Generic Comparison Engine: implement deterministic diffs for model states and analysis runs, including stable-ID mapping, manual mapping, tolerance profiles, and tabular/graphical output.
Epic 5 Handoff Package Generator: implement canonical model export, manifests, hashes, warnings, unresolved assumptions, entity ID mappings, and target mapping metadata.
Epic 6 Design Knowledge and Constraint Engine: implement routing corridors, no-go volumes, support zones, clearance checks, equipment interfaces, and explicit design-knowledge records.
Epic 7 Agent Operation Framework: implement structured operations, schema validation, diff preview, user acceptance, rationale capture, and audit trail.

Future agents should avoid pulling into the MVP, unless the owner reprioritizes: commercial stress software output parsers, automatic external prover comparison, formal prover lifecycle/status enforcement, automatic professional acceptance records, dynamic analysis modules, comprehensive CAD/BIM integration, advanced route optimization, automatic code-compliance claims, and cloud-dependent workflows.
The new PRD explicitly defers comprehensive external-prover result ingestion and forced prover status while preserving future external result states as an architectural possibility.

Future agents should not discard original scope intentionally preserved by the new PRD: full analytical piping stress engine, 3D frame/line-element solver, six-degree-of-freedom nodes, and pipe/bend/branch/rigid-component/reducer/expansion-joint concepts.

Preserved original scope also includes linear and nonlinear supports, fundamental stress recovery, load cases and combinations, user-supplied rule packs, private material/component libraries, unit safety, and no silent engineering defaults.
Preserved original scope also includes IP/data separation, validation benchmarks, auditable reports, and local-first operation.
The project still follows the original intent of open mechanics and private code data, but now adds design-engine scope, state comparison, handoff, and external professional validation boundaries.

When changing development scope, future agents should treat OpenPipeStress_PRD_v0.2.md as shifting the project from an open piping stress analysis platform to an analysis-grade piping design engine with a full stress-analysis core, schema-backed physical model, GUI/agent-assisted iteration, immutable model states, deterministic comparison, and handoff packages for downstream professional validation.
The solver remains essential; what changed is the surrounding product architecture and the authority boundary.
